title: Writing an email
why: After learning to introduce themselves at work, the learner writes their first professional emails: opening, closing, attaching a file, following up and apologizing. The lesson also shows when to use tú or usted, a question on which Spain is far more relaxed than many learners expect.

{"lessons": ["

Opening and closing an email

Good news: Spanish business emails are short and direct, much like in English. No long, flowery formulas: two words are enough to sign off.

The greeting

RegisterTo startTo end
formal (first contact, government offices)Estimado señor Vidal: / Estimada señora Ruiz:Saludos cordiales / Atentamente
neutral (the most common)Hola, Lucía: / Buenos días:Un saludo / Saludos
close coworkerHola, Pablo: / ¡Hola, Pablo!Un abrazo

After the greeting, Spanish uses a colon, not the comma common in English emails: Estimada señora Ruiz:, then a new line starting with a capital letter. Estimado agrees: estimado for a man, estimada for a woman, estimados for a group.

Tú or usted?

English just has \"you,\" but in Spanish you have to choose. In the Spanish workplace, people switch to tú very quickly, a bit like going by first names: between coworkers it's almost always tú, and often with regular clients too. Keep usted for a formal first contact, government offices or an older person. If the other person writes back using tú, follow their lead.

With túWith usted
Te escribo para…Le escribo para…
Te envío el informe.Le envío el informe.
Quedo a la espera de tu respuesta.Quedo a la espera de su respuesta.
¿Podrías llamarme?¿Podría llamarme?
", "

The body of the email: useful phrases

A good Spanish email has three parts: why you're writing, what you're sending or asking for, and what you expect. Here are the phrases that come up again and again.

To…SpanishEnglish
say why you're writingLe escribo para confirmar la reunión.I'm writing to confirm the meeting.
refer to an earlier exchangeLe escribo en relación con su consulta.I'm writing regarding your inquiry.
attach a fileAdjunto le envío el presupuesto. / Te adjunto la factura.Please find the quote attached. / I'm attaching the invoice.
ask politely¿Podría enviarme el contrato?Could you send me the contract?
offer your helpPara cualquier duda, estoy a su disposición.Please don't hesitate to contact me with any questions.
thank in advanceGracias de antemano.Thanks in advance.
ask for a replyQuedo a la espera de su respuesta.I look forward to your reply.

In Adjunto le envío…, adjunto means \"attached.\" You can also use the verb adjuntar (to attach), which is regular: Te adjunto el archivo.

An email is el correo or el correo electrónico (you'll also hear el email). The subject line is el asunto, never \"el sujeto.\" And an attachment is el archivo adjunto.

Asunto: Presupuesto para la feria de MálagaSubject: Quote for the Málaga trade fair
", "

Following up, asking, apologizing

Following up without being curt

To follow up with someone, Spanish stays direct but friendly. The perfect tense (perfecto) is ideal for asking whether something has been done yet:

¿Has podido ver mi correo del lunes?Have you had a chance to look at my email from Monday?
Te recuerdo que el plazo termina el viernes.Just a reminder that the deadline is Friday.

Recordar has a stem change like poder: recuerdo, recuerdas, recuerda, recordamos, recordáis, recuerdan.

Apologizing for a late reply

You reuse the polite imperatives you already know: perdona (tú) and disculpe (usted).

  • Perdona el retraso en contestar. (Sorry for the late reply.)
  • Disculpe la demora. (Please excuse the delay.) La demora is more formal than el retraso.
  • Lo siento, esta semana he estado muy liado. (Sorry, I've been swamped this week.) Liado / liada is informal but very common between coworkers.

A complete email

Hola, Marta: Perdona el retraso en contestar. Te adjunto el informe de marzo. ¿Podrías enviarme la factura antes del viernes? Gracias de antemano. Un saludo, SergioHi Marta, sorry for the late reply. I'm attaching the March report. Could you send me the invoice before Friday? Thanks in advance. Best, Sergio

False friend: contestar means \"to answer, to reply,\" not \"to contest.\" Contestar un correo = to reply to an email; you can also say responder.
